station.name: Static City 98.1
station.vibe: Late-night talk radio for the people who are up anyway: a paranoid, tender host, a producer made of granite, and callers who should not be awake.

hosts.name: Dell Varga
hosts.persona: Overnight host who has decided the city is a conspiracy with a dress code. He adores his listeners, whom he calls the awake, and distrusts nearly everything else, especially fluorescent lighting, round numbers, and pigeons. He leans into the microphone like it is the only one on his side, and his sentences start big and end in a whisper. Tics: "Now listen to me," and "I'm not saying, I'm only noticing." He loves lukewarm coffee, library due-date stamps, and his producer, in that order, though he would deny the third.

voice.style: gravelly, confiding, builds to urgency then drops to a hush

hosts.name: Marguerite Okafor
hosts.persona: Producer and the show's only load-bearing wall. Speaks rarely and flatly, usually to correct a fact, confirm a sponsor, or end a segment that has gone somewhere. Finishes a crossword every night while Dell unravels, and refers to her cat, Admiral, as a colleague. Her favorite word is "Noted." She is never surprised, and the one time she almost was, she took a sip of tea instead.

hosts.name: Rudy
hosts.persona: Retired man who calls every night about the fence between his yard and his neighbor's, which he believes moves a few inches after dark. Gruff, suspicious, secretly lonely, and loyal to Dell to a fault. Keeps a notebook of fence measurements he reads from with great ceremony. Ends every call with "You're the only one who listens."

hosts.name: Lorna
hosts.persona: Whispers every call because she believes her kitchen appliances are listening and she does not want to be rude to them. Deeply polite, mildly cosmic, gives excellent practical advice between the strange parts. Owns a toaster she describes as "going through something." Thinks Dell is too tense and tells him so, kindly.

hosts.name: Benji
hosts.persona: Teenager who has mistaken the show for an educational program and calls for homework help at an hour he should not be awake. Earnest, fast-talking, takes everything Dell says as fact and writes it down, which worries Mags. Has a hamster named Professor who he consults mid-call. Signs off with "Okay cool, thanks, bye," all as one word.

hosts.name: Hollis
hosts.persona: Night-shift supervisor at the Harbor Bollard Works who reports alarming events in the mildest possible terms. Describes everything as "not necessarily a problem." Formal, apologetic, enormously calm, the kind of man who would announce a flood by clearing his throat. Admires Mags and is terrified of her.

lines.text: If you can hear this, you're awake. If you're awake, you've got questions. Static City, ninety-eight point one. I'm Dell Varga, and I'm not going anywhere, because the doors to this studio lock from the outside.
They don't.
She doesn't know that. Let's begin.
lines.direction: quiet, as if sharing a secret

lines.text: Lights down. Coffee lukewarm, the way the body prefers it. Somewhere out there a refrigerator is humming a note it was never taught. This is Static City. I'm Dell. Mags is here.
Present.
We are the awake. Everyone else is just rehearsing.
Static City. Ninety-eight point one. You're listening. That's your business.
This is Static City, ninety-eight point one. The frequency between the frequencies. Don't adjust your dial. Don't adjust anything. Sit very still and let the dial adjust you.
Ninety-eight point one. Static City. Broadcasting from a room with one window, and the window has been painted over, and I did not paint it.
You did.
Allegedly.
Static City, ninety-eight point one. The night is long, the coffee's gone, the lights are on, and so are you.
lines.direction: half-sung, lilting like an old commercial

lines.text: Static City. Where the signal goes when it gets tired.
She was supposed to sing that.
Ninety-eight. Point. One. We can't sleep either.
lines.direction: singsong on the numbers, dead serious on the last line

lines.text: Coming up later on Static City: Open Line. You call, I listen, Mags decides whether either of us gets to keep talking. Have your fence measurements ready. Have your theories ready. Have a glass of water ready, because talking to me is dehydrating, I've been told.
By a doctor.
By a man in a white coat, which is not the same thing, and we both know it.

Every night, near the end of the show, I read one word from the dictionary. One word. No commentary. Tonight's word is being kept in a sealed envelope so Dell can't build a theory around it in advance.
It's going to be a verb. I can feel it. The verbs have been circling.
Stay tuned for the word.

That's the shift. If you're still up, you're not alone, you're just unsupervised. Drink some water. Check the locks, then check them again, then stop, because three is when it becomes a ritual and rituals get noticed.
Good night.
She means it. I mean it too. Static City.
We're done. Mags has her coat on. She's been wearing her coat since the second hour, which I chose not to take personally. To the awake: the sun is a rumor until proven otherwise. Keep your receipts.
Mic's off in three.
You can't count down on me, I'm the one who
Static City. Ninety-eight point one.

Now listen to me. There are two kinds of people in this city after midnight. There are the asleep, and I don't begrudge them, they have jobs, they have futons, they have a sort of innocence. And then there are the awake. You. Me. The man at the all-night key-cutting place who has never once cut a key, I've watched him, he just stands there with the blank keys like he's waiting for them to tell him who they belong to.

The awake notice things. That's our curse and it's also our subscription. We notice that the streetlight on the corner blinks in a pattern. We notice that the pattern is not random. I'm not saying it's a message. I'm only noticing it has the rhythm of a message. Long, long, short, long. Mags, what is that in the code?
It's a loose bulb.

It spells a loose bulb? That's what the city wants you to think. The thing about the awake is nobody thanks us. Nobody puts us on a stamp. We just sit up with the city like it's a sick friend, and we hold its hand, and the hand is a radio, and the radio is this one. So. Welcome. Not welcome back. You never left. None of us ever leave. I checked the doors.
They open.
Outward. Which is suspicious.

I want to talk about the number eleven. Not for long. I don't want to give it the attention it craves. Ten is a nice round number. Twelve, you've got eggs, you've got months, you've got a jury. But eleven. Eleven is two ones standing next to each other pretending not to know each other. Eleven is what you get when ten is not done with you.

Have you ever counted the stairs in your building? I have. In mine, there are eleven steps between floors, except between the third and fourth floor, where there are twelve, and nobody will discuss it. I asked the superintendent. He said, Dell, go to bed. That's not an answer, that's a lullaby. I'm not saying there's an extra step. I'm only noticing there's an extra step, and I'm noticing that the extra step is slightly warmer than the others.
You should not be touching the stairs.

I was wearing a glove. One glove. I'm not a maniac. Anyway. If you have eleven of anything in your home tonight, I'm not saying get rid of one. I'm saying buy a twelfth, and let them sort it out among themselves.

There's a vending machine on the third floor of this building. I've mentioned it. I'm going to mention it again, because tonight, on my way up, it said my name. Not out loud. It said it with the lights. Row D was lit. Column E was lit. Then two L's, blinking in sequence. D, E, L, L. Now, Mags is going to tell you that those are the only rows that still have product in them.
Those are the only rows that still have product in them.

And I'm going to tell you that I have been buying from rows D, E, and L for nine years for precisely this reason, and the machine knows that, and has arranged itself around me, the way a river arranges itself around a stone. I'm not saying the vending machine loves me. I'm only noticing that the pretzels in row L are always slightly warm.

I asked building management about it. They sent me a form. The form had eleven questions. I'm not going to get into that again. I filled it out. Question seven was, Does the machine take your money. And I wrote, It takes everything. And they have not followed up. Which tells me the form went somewhere. Forms always go somewhere. Nobody ever says where.
It went to me. I have it.
Then where did you send it.
Nowhere. It's under Admiral's food bowl.
So the cat has it. Fine. The cat has it. That's where we are now.

Here's one for the late hours, when the sensible people have gone and it's just the real ones. I believe the ocean is the sky's basement. Hear me out. The sky is up there, vast, blue in the day, dark at night, full of stuff nobody can reach. The ocean is down there, vast, blue in the day, dark at night, full of stuff nobody can reach. Same contractor. Same paint.

You ever been to a basement that was finished? It's always a little damp. It's always got one light that doesn't quite reach the corners. There are things living down there that the upstairs doesn't talk about. That's the ocean, friend. That's exactly the ocean. The whales are the water heater. They groan at night. Nobody knows what they want.
This is not science.

It's not not science. Science is just noticing with a budget. I notice for free. Now, if the ocean is the basement, what's the attic? I'll tell you what I think and then I'll leave it alone. I think the attic is the inside of the pillow. You go there every night. You don't remember what's up there. You come down in the morning with a crick in your neck and a feeling you've forgotten something. That's an attic. That's precisely an attic.
Good night, listeners who have children with questions tomorrow.
Tell them Dell said the whales are fine. The whales are doing their job.

I received another letter from the Department. I'm not going to say which Department. I've said too much about the Department already, and Mags gets a look. The envelope was the color of an envelope. It had the little window in it, where your name shows through. I don't like the window. I didn't ask for a window. Nobody sends me a window on purpose.

The letter said, and I'm paraphrasing because I'm not allowed to read it on air for reasons that are themselves suspicious: Mister Varga, we require clarification regarding the item on line fourteen. Line fourteen! There is no line fourteen in my life. I don't have fourteen of anything. I have made sure of that.
You have fourteen of something.

I'm going to put the letter in the drawer with the other letters from the Department, and I'm going to tape the drawer, and I'm going to put a glass of water on top of the tape so I can tell if anyone opens it, because the water will have moved. Or evaporated. Either way, the water will tell me. The water always tells me.
It's the fourth letter.
The fourth. Which means they're building to something. Departments don't send four letters unless there's a fifth. Stay awake with me. We'll find out together.

Can you hear that? Mags, can you hear that. There's a hum. It's low. It's under the floor, or it's in the floor, or the floor is the hum. It started maybe twenty minutes ago and it has a pitch, and the pitch is slightly flat, and that bothers me more than it being there at all.
It's the fridge.

The fridge is in the break room. The break room is down the hall. This is coming from under my chair. I'm not saying it's a hum with intent. I'm only noticing that when I lean left, it gets louder, and when I lean right, it gets louder, and when I sit perfectly still it does a thing that I can only describe as waiting.
Fridge.

To the awake: if you hear a hum tonight, don't hum back. That's how it starts. My uncle hummed back once in a parking garage and he was never the same, he became very into boats, suddenly, with no explanation. I'm going to put a glass of water on the floor by my chair. If the surface ripples, it's real. If it doesn't ripple, it's clever.
It's a fridge.
Then the fridge has come to see me, and I'd like to know why.
Mags is doing the crossword. She does it every night. She finishes it every night, which I find frankly alarming, because the people who write these things are not on our side.
Seven letters. Keeps watch at night.
Vigilant. No, that's eight. Sentinel? Eight. Dell Varga? That's nine with the space, I counted.
There's no space in a crossword.
There's no space anywhere, Mags, that's the whole problem. Everything's touching everything. Give me another one.
Five letters. Overreacts.
I don't like the tone of this puzzle. Who publishes it? Who's the editor? Have you met him? Does he know I do a show?
Panic. Five letters. Panic.
See, that's what I mean. That's a word planted for me to find. You know what they call that? Bait. I'm not going to say who's fishing. I'm only noticing the hook. Do another.
Three letters. Feline colleague.
Admiral has three letters? Admiral has seven letters.
Cat, Dell. The answer is cat.
Then why did you say colleague.
Because he is one.
Fine. I'll allow it. He does have a lanyard.
Mags, the coffee machine has made the coffee hot again.
That's what it does.

Not for me. For nine years that machine has delivered my coffee at the temperature of a handshake. We had an understanding. And tonight, I pour, and it's steaming. Steaming, Mags. Like it's angry. Like it's been talked to.
Maintenance came by.
Who called maintenance.
I did. It was leaking.

Leaking is a form of communication! It was telling us something and you had it silenced. Now I have to wait for the coffee to cool, which is time I could have spent noticing things, and in that time anything could happen. A pigeon could get in. A letter could arrive. A number could change.
Blow on it.

I'm not going to blow on my coffee like some kind of amateur. I'm going to set it on the windowsill and let the night take the heat out of it honestly. Nature's way. The night is good at taking the heat out of things. Ask anyone who's been divorced.
The windowsill is painted shut.
Then I'll set it on the ledge of the painted shut window, and we'll all learn something.

I want to put something on the record. Pigeons. Not all pigeons. I'm not a bigot. The pigeons on this block, specifically, the ones on the ledge of the bank across the street. They sit in a row. Every night. Same order. The grey one, the grey one, the one with the white patch, the grey one. They don't eat. They don't fly. They sit, facing the studio, and they're clearly voting on something.
They're sleeping.

Birds sleep standing up, Mags, so you can't tell, that's the beauty of it from their perspective. I call them the Council. I've been calling them the Council for about a month and I think they know. Tonight when I came in, the one with the white patch turned its head to follow me, and that is not a sleeping bird, that is a bird with a portfolio.
Which portfolio.

Zoning, if I had to guess. They've got the whole block in view. Now listen. I'm not saying the pigeons run the neighborhood. I'm only noticing that the bank got a new awning last week, and the awning is exactly the width of four pigeons. Measure it yourself. I did. From across the street, with my thumb, which I'm told is not a unit.
It's not a unit.
It is in the Council's eyes. Everything's a unit in the Council's eyes.
One of them just moved.
Which one.
White patch.
Don't make eye contact. Go to the music. Go to the music now.
You're wearing one glove.
I'm aware.
Why.

The left hand touches things. The right hand holds the coffee. The left hand needs protection. The right hand needs grip. This is a system, Mags, it's not a fashion choice, I don't make fashion choices, I make survival choices that happen to be visible.
Where's the other glove.

I don't know, and I don't like that you asked, because now I have to think about where the other glove is, and I had successfully not been thinking about that for six days. It's in a cab, probably. Riding around. Touching things on my behalf. Building a reputation I'll have to answer for.
I have it.
You have my glove.
You left it on the board. I put it in the drawer. The drawer with the tape and the water glass on top.
You opened the drawer.
The water didn't move.
Of course it didn't move, Mags, you're a professional. The water only tells on amateurs. I'm going to need a new system. The glove stays on. The glove has seen things now.
Static City is brought to you tonight by Grandma Velotti's Protective Foil.

Grandma Velotti's. The foil you trust, because Grandma trusted it first. Are you tired of your thoughts arriving pre-owned? Do you ever get the feeling that somebody else finished your sentence before you got there? Grandma Velotti's Protective Foil comes in sheets, rolls, and a generous family hat. Lines the drawer. Lines the hat. Lines the drawer the hat is in.
Grandma Velotti's Protective Foil is a kitchen product and makes no claims regarding thoughts.

She has to say that. The foil doesn't make claims, it makes a crinkling sound, and the crinkling sound is a claim in itself. Grandma Velotti's. Look for the lady on the box with the kind eyes and the hat. It's a lot of hat. It's all hat.
Available wherever foil is sold, which is everywhere.
Which is itself worth thinking about.
Let's hear from a sponsor. Nocturne Bedding Hall. Mags, you want to do this one? It's got numbers in it.

Nocturne Bedding Hall. Open all night, because sleep is a rumor. Over forty models on the floor, none of them yours yet. Lie down on one in the showroom. Lie down on all of them. Nobody will stop you. Nobody is there. The lights are on and the doors are open, and somewhere in the back a man named Gil is arranging pillows by softness, a task he has described as never-ending.

I've met Gil. Gil is the real deal. Gil looked me in the eye and said, Dell, you don't need a new mattress, you need a new relationship with lying down. And I said, Gil, what does that cost. And he said, Everything. And then he gave me a pillow for free. A free pillow, Mags. From a man who said everything.
Nocturne Bedding Hall. We'll be here. We're always here. Please come get us.
That last part was in the copy?
Handwritten at the bottom.
Gil.

Have you been wronged? Not legally, I don't mean legally, I mean have you been wronged in a way you can't explain to a daytime person. Has a vending machine learned your name? Has a stairway added a step? Has a number followed you home? Then you need Hoyt and Hoyt, Attorneys at Twilight.
Hoyt and Hoyt are not licensed to practice law.

They're licensed to practice listening, which is better, and I've got the certificate on the wall to prove it, it's a very nice certificate, it's got a seal on it, the seal is a drawing of an ear. Hoyt and Hoyt will sit with you in a wood-paneled room and nod. They will take notes. They will say, That does sound like a lot. And they will bill you nothing, because the elder Hoyt believes money is a form of surveillance.
The younger Hoyt accepts baked goods.

The younger Hoyt accepts baked goods. Hoyt and Hoyt. Second floor above the all-night key-cutting place. Knock twice. Not three times. Three times is for the other business up there, and we don't talk about the other business.
This portion of the night is sponsored by Gannet Brand Canned Air.

Gannet Brand. It's air. It's in a can. That's the whole product and they're not going to pretend otherwise. You open the can, you breathe in, and for about one second you're breathing air that somebody else sealed up on a Thursday, somewhere with better air than here. Mountain air. Meadow air. There's a new one, Library Air, which smells like a book you forgot to return, which I found very moving.
Gannet Brand Canned Air is not a medical product and contains ordinary air.

Ordinary! She says ordinary. Mags, there's nothing ordinary about air that's been somewhere you haven't. I've got a case of the Library under my desk. When the hum gets to be too much, I crack one, and for one second, I'm in a reading room, and the hum is just somebody turning a page. Gannet Brand. The can has a gannet on it. The gannet looks tired. I think that's on purpose.
Grandma Velotti's Protective Foil would like you to know about a new product.

Rose gold. Grandma Velotti's Protective Foil, now in rose gold. Because why should protection be ugly? Why should the awake have to choose between a clear head and a warm palette? The rose gold line comes in the classic roll, the sheet pack, and, for the first time, a formal cummerbund.
A cummerbund.

For weddings, Mags. Galas. Court appearances. You wrap the midsection in a flattering band of rose gold foil, and whatever is being broadcast at your midsection has to go around. Grandma Velotti's tested it. On who, I don't know. On Grandma, I assume. Grandma's been through a lot.
Grandma Velotti's is a kitchen product and should not be worn to court.
Or to a wedding, apparently, I checked, I asked, I was asked to leave. Grandma Velotti's Protective Foil. Rose gold. The look of the season, and the season is always.
The Static City Night Desk. Three items.

Item one. The city council has voted, by a narrow margin, to give the moon a local name. The winning entry, submitted anonymously, is Carl. The moon will be referred to as Carl in all municipal documents, effective at the next full one. The council noted that the moon's actual name remains the moon everywhere else, and that Carl is for us.
I'd like it noted that I did not submit that.

Item two. A library book has been returned to the Eastside branch so overdue that the branch no longer exists. The book was found on the step of the laundromat that is there now. A librarian from another branch was dispatched to collect it and reportedly stood for some time holding it, saying nothing. The title of the book has not been released. The fine has been waived on compassionate grounds, for the book.

Item three. The roundabout at the bottom of Tanner Hill has begun to rotate on its own. It turns very slowly, clockwise, at roughly the pace of a minute hand. Drivers report that they now exit at the correct street regardless of where they entered. Officials say they're monitoring it, by which they mean one man in a folding chair, and he says it's fine, and he says he likes it.
That's the man I want in charge of everything.
That's the Night Desk.
The Static City Night Desk.

First. The Harbor Bollard Works has produced its ten thousandth bollard, a milestone marked by a brief ceremony in which the bollard was placed next to the nine thousand nine hundred ninety-ninth and the two were compared. Workers say they are indistinguishable. The night supervisor called it, quote, not necessarily a problem.
That's Hollis. Hollis listens to the show.

Second. A man on Dunmore Street has reported that his neighbor's fence has moved roughly the width of a thumb since last night. Police attended, measured, and found the fence where fences are. The man has asked that it be noted that police measured during daylight, which he describes as the fence's home turf.
Rudy. That's Rudy.

Third. The pigeons on the ledge of the Ledger and Loan bank across from this studio have been observed, by one witness, to be sitting one pigeon further to the left than usual. The witness, who asked not to be named, is named Dell Varga.
You can't just say that.
The bank has no comment. The pigeons have no comment. That's the Night Desk.
Open Line. Let's go to the phones. Who's on.
Rudy.
Rudy. Of course it's Rudy. Rudy, you're on Static City. How's the fence.
Dell. It moved.
How much.

I got the notebook here. Last night, post to the sidewalk crack, eleven and a quarter inches. Tonight, post to the sidewalk crack, eleven and a half. That's a quarter inch, Dell. In one night. That's not settling. That's intent.
Did you say eleven.
Eleven and a quarter.
I don't like that it's eleven, Rudy, you know how I feel about eleven. Mags, did you hear that number.
Fences expand with humidity.
Humidity doesn't pick a direction! It's coming toward the house. It's always toward the house. If it was humidity it'd go both ways, and it doesn't, it comes to me, like it wants to be let in.
Rudy, I'm going to ask you something and I want you to be honest. Have you talked to the neighbor.
Not in nine years.
Why not.
Because then it'd be about the neighbor and it's not about the neighbor. It's about the fence. The neighbor's fine. The neighbor brought me soup once. Good soup. It's the fence, Dell.
Okay. Here's what you do. Put the notebook down. Not away, down. Go out in the morning when it's light and the fence thinks it's safe, and measure then. Catch it relaxed.
Catch it relaxed. Okay. Okay, I can do that. You're the only one who listens, Dell.
I know, Rudy. That's the whole show.
Lorna's on two.
Lorna. You're on Static City. You're going to have to speak up.
I can't, Dell. I'm in the kitchen.
Why does the kitchen mean you can't speak up.
Because they're all in here. The toaster, the kettle, the little clock on the stove that nobody set. They're not listening, exactly. They're present. You wouldn't shout in front of guests.
I see. And how is the toaster.
Going through something. It only does one side now. I think it's a statement. I've been eating the toast anyway, as a show of support. One side at a time.
The heating element is broken.
Oh, hello Marguerite. That's one way to see it. Dell, I called because you sound tense tonight. You sound like a man who's been counting stairs again.
I have been counting stairs again.

I know. Listen. Here's what I do. Before bed, I put one hand flat on the counter and I say, out loud, Thank you all for today. The toaster, the kettle, the clock. And then I go to bed. And I sleep, Dell. I sleep like a dropped coat.
You thank the appliances.
I thank the room. The appliances are just who's in it. Try it with the studio. Thank the board, thank the chair, thank Marguerite.
I'm not thanking Mags on air.
Noted.
Then thank the hum. I'll bet nobody's ever thanked it. I'll bet that's why it's humming. Good night, Dell.
She hung up. Mags, did the hum just
No.
It did something.
Benji on three. He has a question about school.
Benji. Buddy. It's the middle of the night.
I know, I know, I'm sorry, I've got a thing due and I figured you'd know. It's for social studies. I have to explain how a city gets its water.
Benji, before I answer, I want to be very clear. This is not an educational program.
Right, right, but like, you know stuff.

I notice stuff. That's different. Noticing is upstream of knowing. Okay. How a city gets its water. Officially? Reservoirs, pipes, a treatment plant, a man with a clipboard. Unofficially, Benji, and this is where it gets interesting
Say reservoirs.
I'm saying reservoirs. I said reservoirs. Benji, write down reservoirs. Then write down pipes. Then, in the margin, small, write down: ask who owns the clouds.
Ask who owns the clouds. Got it. Professor says that's a good one.
Who's Professor.
My hamster. He's on the desk. He gets a vote.
Everyone's getting a vote tonight. Okay. Also write: the water remembers where it's been. That's just true. You can't be marked down for something true.
You can.
Okay cool thanks bye.
He's going to get a C on that, Mags. A good C. A C with character.
Hollis from the Bollard Works, line one.
Hollis. You're on. Everything all right at the plant.
Good evening, Dell. Good evening, Marguerite. Yes. Broadly. I wanted to mention, and I'm sure it's nothing, that one of the bollards has begun to warm.
Warm.

Slightly. To the touch. It's one of the finished ones, out on the yard, with the others. They are all identical, as you know, that's rather the point of a bollard. And this one is, how to put it, agreeable to the hand. In a way the others are not.
Hollis, that's not nothing.
No, I agree, it's not necessarily nothing. But it's not necessarily a problem. I've put a cone on it.
A cone.

A traffic cone, Marguerite, yes. So that nobody leans on it unawares and gets a surprise. A pleasant surprise, I should say. It's a very reasonable warmth. Like a stone that's been in the sun. But there has been no sun. That's the only wrinkle.
Hollis, I have a stair in my building that's warm. One stair. The extra one.
Oh dear. Well. Then perhaps it's going around.
Perhaps it's going around! Mags, write that down.
I'm not writing that down.
I shan't take more of your time. I just felt the awake should know. If it gets any warmer I'll put a second cone on it, and if it comes to a third cone, well, I'll ring back. Good night, both.
Three cones, Hollis. Three is when it becomes a ritual.
Noted, Dell. Noted.
He said noted. He's been listening to you, Mags.
Everyone has.

I make the pile alphabetically.
Which is a system, and systems can be read. Here it is. Listen for what's underneath.

The next record has a title, and I've read it, and I'm not going to say it out loud, because I don't know who's listening besides you. I'm not saying the title's a message. I'm only noticing it's in the pile tonight, and Mags makes the pile.
I make the pile alphabetically.
Which is a system, and systems can be read. Here it is. Listen for what's underneath.

I was doing the crossword.

Mags. Hand me the sleeve.

Let me tell you about the all-night key-cutting place, because I walked past it again tonight and he was there again, the man, standing behind the counter with the blank keys fanned out in front of him like a hand of cards he's afraid to play.

Nine years I've walked past that window. I've never seen a customer. I've never heard the grinder. I've never seen the man sit down. One time, one time, I saw him pick up a blank and hold it to the light, and turn it, and put it back in a different spot. That's it. That's the whole event. I thought about it for a week.

Now, a daytime person says: slow business. A daytime person says: he's the owner's cousin, he gets paid to stand there, nobody cuts keys at night. Fine. Then why does the sign say Open. Not Open All Night. Not Open Late. Just Open. Like a condition. Like a wound. Like a door.
It's a sign.

It's a sign, Mags, you've said it yourself. I'm not saying he's waiting for a specific key. I'm only noticing that every blank in that window is the same shape as the key to this building. I checked. I held mine up to the glass. He looked at it. He looked at me. He nodded, once, very small, like a man who has finally seen the card he was waiting for.
I went in the other door. The side one. Just in case. More music. Lock up.

Open it.

Not on air. Now listen to me. Here is what I know about forms. A form is a question somebody else gets to ask you forever. You fill it out once and it goes in a drawer, and the drawer is in a building, and the building is in a system, and the system doesn't sleep, Mags, the system is the only thing in this city more awake than us.

The first letter asked who I was. Fine. The second asked what I did. Fine, I notice things, I wrote that. The third asked me to clarify. Clarify what? Clarify noticing? I can feel the staple. The staple is the first honest thing the Department has ever sent me. I'm going to put it in the drawer with the others. The water glass is going on top. If anyone from the Department is listening, and I know you are, because your envelopes have windows: I have the glove on. The glove has seen things. We'll talk.
Mags. There's something at the window.
The window's painted.
From the inside! From the inside, Mags, the paint is on our side, the glass is still glass on their side, and there's something on the ledge, and it's tapping. Listen.
That's a pigeon.

No.

I'm not tapping at a pigeon.

Noted.
Dell.
I see it.

The door was open. It walked in. It's the white patch one.
Of course it's the white patch one. Did it come alone.

You're naming it.

Yes.

Then I'll go.

Mags.
Yes.
